abstract:
Automated survey generation systems increasingly rely on flat retrieval over document collections, limiting their ability to capture the evolutionary structure of research fields. We present SurveyGraph, a framework centered on a Methods-Entity Knowledge Graph (MEKG) that encodes method-level follow-on, competition, and shared-resource relations across papers. The MEKG serves as a unified backbone for core-paper discovery, graph-aware retrieval, hybrid outline generation, and evolutionary narrative synthesis.

We evaluate SurveyGraph through a multi-level protocol spanning retrieval benchmarks, semantic-edge validation, citation grounding audits, benchmark-facing collection probes, and same-backend generation-stage diagnostics. In a controlled seven-method equal-budget benchmark, MEKG-anchored fusion achieves the best balance of recall and structural density among all tested methods, demonstrating that typed graph structure provides a complementary signal to simpler retrieval approaches. On the archived graph-native core diagnostic, graph-aware retrieval nearly doubles recall over flat lexical baselines across all eight runs ($p{=}0.004$). A semantic evidence gate with AUC=0.75 filters noisy edges, and citation-grounding audits over 160 generated sentences confirm 80.6% anchored-or-partial support with evidence-level contrasts validating genuine alignment. Human validation over 108 stratified semantic edges (Cohen’s $\kappa{=}0.64$ for the binary support decision) confirms 68.5% supported-or-partial after adjudication, with improves relations strongest at 80.6% and extends weakest at 52.8%. A SurveyBench-facing collection probe reaches 0.521 mean reference coverage on four topics under an eight-paper budget; same-backend Qwen diagnostics over a 30-paper/74-relation MEKG further show that removing hybrid outlining lowers artifact organization signals. We report concurrent-system comparisons only as bounded diagnostics rather than same-backend end-to-end claims. Code and artifacts are available at: https://github.com/xzzvsxd/SurveyGraph.

sections.body: The authors argue that flat retrieval over papers cannot capture which work extends which idea or where methods split into competing families. They propose SurveyGraph, which uses a Methods-Entity Knowledge Graph (MEKG) with typed follow-on, competition and shared-resource relations to drive core-paper discovery, graph-aware retrieval, hybrid outlining and narrative synthesis. The stated contributions are a seven-method retrieval benchmark, a graph-native diagnostic with p=0.004, citation-grounding audits at 80.6% anchored-or-partial, human validation with Cohen's kappa of 0.64 on 108 edges, and released artifacts.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Flat retrieval in survey generation misses how methods evolve, so SurveyGraph builds a typed method graph to recover that structure.

sections.body: Related work covers multi-stage survey generators such as AutoSurvey, SurveyX, SurveyForge and SciSage, and concurrent structure-first systems such as MVSS and StructSurvey. It also lists benchmarks including SurGE, SurveyBench and DeepSurvey-Bench, along with graph-centric scholarly tools. The authors name two differences: the central representation is a method-entity evolutionary graph rather than a generic citation graph, and that graph serves retrieval, outlining and generation as one backbone.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Related work groups survey generators, benchmarks and graph tools, and differs by using one method-entity graph across the full pipeline.

sections.body: The pipeline has four stages: MEKG construction, hybrid outline generation, Graph-RAG retrieval and evolutionary narrative synthesis. The graph has six entity types and 21 typed relations in five categories. Core papers are scored with fixed hand-tuned weights of 0.4, 0.3, 0.2 and 0.1 rather than learned ones. Outlines fuse a top-down template with HDBSCAN clusters, and retrieval uses 1-hop traversal with k=5 papers per relation type. The paper states that the saved runs expose only a subset of the relation families, so retrieval analyses use only those present.
sections.heading: The SurveyGraph Framework
sections.headline: The framework builds a Methods-Entity Knowledge Graph and reuses it for outlining, retrieval and narrative synthesis.

sections.body: Graph-native metrics measure how strongly a generated survey tracks the MEKG. Weighted Centrality Recall (WCR) is coverage of core papers weighted by their importance score. Community Coverage (CC) counts the graph communities represented, and Structural Coherence (SC) is the fraction of communities matched by at least one outline section title. Benchmark alignment draws metrics from SurGE, SurveyBench, SurveyLens, DeepSurvey-Bench and ReportBench. The internal evaluator adds checks across five dimensions.
sections.heading: Evaluation Framework
sections.headline: Evaluation separates graph-native diagnostics, retrieval benchmarks, grounding audits and benchmark alignment into distinct levels.

sections.body: Eight SurveyGraph runs were compared with flat lexical retrieval under a top-5 per-section budget. On the archived graph-native target set, core-paper recall rose from 0.216 to 0.373 with a sign test of p=0.004. Removing 1-hop expansion dropped recall to 0.219, and the authors flag this as a mechanism diagnostic because the targets are graph-derived. In a seven-method equal-budget benchmark, MEKG-anchored fusion raised relation density while keeping competitive recall. The evidence gate has an AUC of 0.75, and human annotation of 108 edges gives a Cohen's kappa of 0.64.
sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.headline: Graph-aware retrieval raises core-paper recall from 0.216 to 0.373 across eight runs, with p=0.004.

sections.body: The conclusion lists three findings. Graph-neighborhood traversal drives the gain over flat retrieval with p=0.004. MEKG-anchored fusion gives a strong recall-structure tradeoff in the seven-method benchmark. Evidence gating with AUC=0.75 and human annotation with kappa of 0.64 show 68.5% of sampled edges are supported-or-partial after adjudication. The stated contribution is an auditable typed structural layer, while SurveyBench results remain collection-stage diagnostics and MVSS and StructSurvey remain contextual comparisons.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The conclusion claims an auditable typed structure layer, while SurveyBench results remain collection-stage diagnostics.

sections.body: The SurveyBench results are collection-stage and reference-list probes, not full end-to-end submissions, and they include no outlining or claim-support evaluation. No evaluation on SurGE or SurveyLens is reported. The 108-edge annotation covers three relation types from a single domain cluster, and three-way label agreement is lower, so ternary labels are used mainly for failure-mode diagnosis. The MVSS and StructSurvey comparison is not a same-backend rerun, so it is not decisive evidence of superiority. The graph-native metrics are diagnostic signals rather than standalone quality measures.
sections.heading: Limitations
sections.headline: SurveyBench results are collection-stage probes, and edge validation rests on 108 edges from one domain cluster.

sections.body: The work uses public scholarly metadata and paper text, with no human-subject experiments or newly collected personal data. The stated main risk is that generation may amplify hallucinated citations, unsupported summaries or plausible but incomplete synthesis. The authors keep graph metrics separate from benchmark-facing evaluation and avoid treating the internal composite score as a proxy for human scholarly judgment. AI assistants were used for code exploration and drafting support, and all reported claims were checked against archived artifacts, logs and reproduced outputs.
sections.heading: Ethical Considerations
sections.headline: Ethical risk is mainly hallucinated citations, and claims were checked against archived artifacts before inclusion.

sections.body: The appendix inventories the released artifacts, including eight completed runs with evaluator traces. Table A.1 gives internal evaluator scores per run with a mean overall of 76.74, and Table A.2 gives graph-native diagnostics. Appendix B reports an offline evaluator replay with an overall score of 78.14 and fresh single-PDF smoke runs with zero relations. Table A.4 reports Qwen generation diagnostics, Table A.5 five-topic pipeline completion, and Table A.6 an artifact-level comparison that the authors say is not a fair live rerun.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists artifacts, reproducibility audits, Qwen generation diagnostics, the SurveyBench probe, the evidence-gate threshold analysis and comparison boundaries.
